title: Triggers and Causes of Feelings
keyIdea: Feelings have causes. Something happens (a trigger) and then we feel a certain way: I felt sad because my balloon popped. The trigger is what happened, not the feeling and not what we did next. A cause can come earlier in the day, or be something we are waiting for. Being tired or hungry can make a feeling bigger.

kid: Feelings do not come from nowhere. Something happens first. Then we feel. The thing that happens is called a trigger.
Mia's ice cream fell on the floor. She felt sad. We can say: Mia felt sad because her ice cream fell.
The trigger is not the feeling. Cross is a feeling. My brother took my toy is the trigger. Crying is what you do after.
Look back! The cause may be from before. Being tired or hungry can make feelings bigger too. What are your triggers?
adult: This topic, for ages 5 to 7, is about understanding that feelings have causes. Something happens, the trigger, and that leads to a feeling. Children practise saying "I felt ___ because ___", finding what made a story character feel a certain way, and noticing what triggers their own feelings.

Three ideas make it work. The trigger is an event, not a feeling word. The cause is not always the thing in front of the child: a child who is grumpy at lunch may be upset about something at playtime, or excited about a party tomorrow. And the body matters: being tired or hungry lowers the threshold, so small things feel big.

Common mistakes: giving the feeling as the cause ("I was sad because I was sad"), giving what they did after ("because I cried"), blaming whatever is nearest in time, and believing feelings just happen for no reason. Be careful not to turn because into blame. The aim is to understand the feeling, and the trigger does not excuse hurting anyone.

In the lab your child matches what happened to three children's feelings, sorts cards into what happened and feelings, looks back through a comic strip to find an earlier cause, checks Ava's sleep and tummy, and builds two "I feel … when …" sentences of their own.

familyTip: At bedtime, share one feeling each from the day with a because: "I felt proud because I fixed the gate." When your child is upset, wait until they are calm, then ask "What happened just before?" and "Are you tired or hungry?"

practice.prompt: Sam felt scared. What was the trigger?
choices: A big dog barked at him
practice.hint: The trigger is what happened first, before the feeling.
practice.explain: The dog barking is the trigger. Hiding is what Sam did after, and scared is the feeling.

practice.prompt: Jo builds a tower of {n} blocks. It falls down. Jo feels cross. What is the trigger?
choices: The tower of {n} blocks fell down
practice.hint: Which one happened first and made Jo feel cross?
practice.explain: The tower falling is the trigger. Cross is the feeling. Kicking is what Jo did after.
"I felt sad because my balloon popped" names the trigger. Crying came after the feeling.

practice.prompt: Ravi waits {n} minutes for a turn on the swing. Then he gets a turn. How might he feel, and why?
choices: Happy, because he got his turn
Sad, because he got his turn
practice.hint: Name a feeling, then say what made it happen.
practice.explain: Ravi feels happy because he got his turn. Getting his turn is the cause.

practice.prompt: Leo is grumpy at lunch. Lunch is pasta, and he likes pasta. At playtime his ball went over the fence. What made him grumpy?
choices: His ball went over the fence
practice.hint: Look back. What happened before lunch?
practice.explain: Losing his ball at playtime made Leo grumpy. A cause can come earlier than the feeling shows.

choices: My friend would not play with me
pool.hint: A trigger is something that happens to you.
pool.explain: "My friend would not play with me" is a trigger. Lonely is a feeling. Stamping is what someone did.

pool.hint: A feeling is inside you. It is a word like glad, sad or cross.
pool.explain: Worried is a feeling. The cat running away and losing a shoe are things that happened.

pool.hint: What happened that made Mia proud?
pool.explain: Mia felt proud because she finished her puzzle. Smiling shows the feeling. It is not the cause.

pool.prompt: Ben slept only {n} hours last night. Today a small thing makes him very cross. What can make the feeling bigger?
pool.hint: Think about his body. Did he get enough sleep?
pool.explain: Being tired can make feelings bigger. With only {n} hours of sleep, a small thing can feel big.

pool.prompt: Zara feels excited at bedtime. Her party is tomorrow. What is the cause?
pool.hint: A cause can be something you are waiting for.
pool.explain: Zara is excited because her party is tomorrow. Something coming up can cause a feeling too.

pool.prompt: Amy gets {n} stickers for helping. She feels glad. Which sentence is right?
choices: Amy felt glad because she got {n} stickers
Amy got {n} stickers because she felt glad
Amy felt glad because she was glad
pool.hint: The feeling comes after what happened.
pool.explain: Amy felt glad because she got {n} stickers. Getting the stickers came first, then the feeling.

pool.hint: After because, say what happened first.
pool.explain: "I heard a strange noise" is the trigger. Hiding is what you did after the feeling.

pool.prompt: Tom and Kim both hear fireworks. Tom feels scared. Kim feels excited. What is true?
choices: One trigger can cause different feelings
One of them has the wrong feeling
pool.hint: Can two people feel different things about the same thing?
pool.explain: One trigger can cause different feelings in different people. Neither feeling is wrong.

visual.caption: What happened, or a feeling? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match causes to feelings, sort triggers from feelings, look back for a cause, check tired and hungry, make your own.
